title: Who was Paul?
summary: Acts portrays Paul as a former persecutor who becomes a missionary, while Paul’s letters explain his call and the message he proclaims. The cited texts emphasize different parts of his work: announcing the gospel among the nations, teaching churches, and bearing witness to Jesus’ resurrection.
historical_context: Acts narrates Paul’s change of direction and his sending from Antioch; Galatians 1 gives Paul’s own account of his call and earlier persecution. Romans, 1 Corinthians, and Philippians show how he presents his message and addresses communities. These references offer distinct narrative and letter perspectives rather than a complete chronology of Paul’s life.
canonical_context: Acts 9 narrates Paul’s encounter and changed course, and Acts 13 depicts the community at Antioch sending Barnabas and Saul. In Galatians 1, Paul recounts his former persecution and says he was called to proclaim Christ among the nations. Romans 1 describes his commission and the gospel’s reach to both Jew and Greek; 1 Corinthians 15 summarizes the resurrection message and Paul’s place among its witnesses; Philippians 3 reframes his former credentials in light of knowing Christ. Second Timothy 4 presents Paul in a final-charge setting. The passages address different questions and should not be treated as a single uninterrupted biography.
literary_context: Acts tells Paul’s story in third-person narrative, while Galatians 1 gives his first-person account of his call and past. Romans 1 opens a letter by introducing its author’s commission and gospel; 1 Corinthians 15 recalls the message received and the witnesses to the resurrection; Philippians 3 uses autobiographical contrast within an argument. Reading each form on its own terms shows what the passage contributes to understanding Paul.
covenantal_significance: The cited passages present Paul’s mission as carrying the message of Jesus beyond Israel: Galatians 1 says he was called to proclaim Christ among the nations, and Romans 1 describes the gospel as for Jew and Greek. First Corinthians 15 centers that message on Jesus’ death, burial, and resurrection. These texts support a mission to the nations; they do not by themselves provide a full account of Paul’s teaching about covenant or the place of Israel.
canonical_role: Who was Paul? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

interpretive_notes.note: Acts and Paul’s letters offer different kinds of evidence. Acts narrates events in Paul’s mission, while Galatians 1 gives Paul’s own account of his call and earlier life. Compare the accounts where they overlap, but do not collapse narrative and letter argument into one voice.

The cited passages show both proclamation and interpretation: Acts 13 depicts Paul being sent on mission, Romans 1 introduces his gospel, 1 Corinthians 15 summarizes the resurrection message, and Philippians 3 explains how he revalues his former status. Each text contributes a particular aspect of his work.
